title: A resources section that is not a blog dump
metaTitle: Resources grouped by the reader's job
excerpt: Group a resources section by the job a reader is trying to finish. A reverse-chronological feed of every post is an archive, and it should not be the front door.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, rooms a visitor can tell apart the way a resources section should be grouped.
caption: A corridor with rooms you can tell apart. Group resources by the job, not by the date. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a resources section be organized?
faqs.answer: Organize it by the jobs readers already ask about, such as choosing, setting up, or shipping. Five to seven groups is enough for most sites. A reverse-chronological list can exist as an archive in the footer of that section.

faqs.question: What should a resource card include?
faqs.answer: A title that states the outcome, one line that is true even if the reader never opens the piece, and a single primary group. Add the format, such as a checklist or a ten-minute read, when the weight of the piece changes the choice.

faqs.question: Who decides which group a new piece joins?
faqs.answer: Name an owner. Without one, every new post lands on the resources front because that is the CMS default. The owner also removes or updates pieces that no longer help someone finish the job.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A resources section helps a reader finish a job. Group the pieces by that job. Pricing questions in one place. Setup in another. Care, shipping, or implementation in a third. Resources page information architecture is the decision of those groups, the names on them, and what you refuse to file there.

A reverse-chronological list of everything you have written is an archive. Keep the archive if you need it. Do not make it the front door.

## Name the jobs before you name the categories

Start with the questions a real reader already asks. A founder buying software asks how to evaluate, how to start, and how to migrate. A shopper asks how to choose a size, how to care for the thing, and how delivery works. A clinic, a school, or a local service asks what to bring, how to book, and what it costs.

Write those questions down from support mail, sales calls, and the lines people type into your own search. Five to seven jobs is a healthy set. Twenty jobs is a second navigation with no priority. If you cannot explain a group in one plain phrase, it is two groups, or it is not a group yet.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a site has a primary purpose, and whether someone can leave having learned enough to achieve a goal. A resources section passes that test when each group has a purpose a stranger can see. It fails when the purpose is "publish on a schedule."

Put the reader's verb in the label. "Choose a plan," "Set it up," "Ship and returns." Labels like "Insights," "Perspectives," and "Resources" postpone the decision. The word resources can be the name of the section. It should not be the name of every shelf inside it.

On a Hanabi project this list is written before the layout. Figma can hold the groups as a simple map. The site, built in Next.js and React, can then render one template for every guide, with the group stored as data rather than as a one-off page. Prisma and PostgreSQL are there when the library is large enough to query. A small library can live as content files. Either way, the groups are a decision, not a theme.

## What belongs on the shelf

A piece belongs if a reader with that job would open it on purpose. A setup guide belongs. A definition that unblocks a purchase belongs. A comparison you can stand behind belongs, if it is specific enough to use.

A piece does not belong just because it exists. Company news, a hiring post, and a campaign recap can live on the journal or the archive. Pulling them onto the resources front steals attention from the guides that do a job.

Give each piece one primary group. A second link is fine when a guide truly serves two jobs. Five links to the same essay, under five vague tags, is how a library becomes a blog dump with extra chrome.

Write a one-line description that states the outcome. "How to read a quote when the number is not public" is a line. "Thoughts on pricing" is a mood. The line should be true even if the title is clever. Many readers never open the piece. The line is the piece, for them.

Date the piece quietly. A guide from three years ago can still be the best answer if the product has not changed. A guide that is wrong should be updated or removed. Changing the date without changing the advice is the kind of false freshness Google's helpful-content notes warn against. Substance first. The date second.

## The first screen of the section

The first screen should show the groups, not the latest post. A reader who lands here from a footer link is in a hurry. Nielsen Norman Group's research on page visits is the right caution: people often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text. Lead with the jobs. The newest essay can have a quiet corner if your regular readers want it. It should not be the only structure.

Order the groups by how often the job blocks a decision. For a product company, start with the job that happens before money changes hands, then setup, then the long-term jobs. For a shop, start with choosing and care, then shipping. Do not order by which post performed last month. Performance is a clue. The reader's sequence is the design.

Each group needs a short introduction of one or two sentences. What this shelf is for. Who it is not for, if that saves a click. Then a handful of links, the best ones, not all of them. A group with forty links needs a second level, or it needs editing.

Show the format when it changes the choice. A ten-minute read, a checklist, a template, a film. People pick differently when they know the weight. Hide the format and they open three things they will not finish, then blame the library.

Include a way back to the offer. A guide that helps someone decide should point at the page where they can act. One link, in the template, to the relevant product, service, or contact path. A resources section that never reconnects to the business is a magazine you are funding by accident.

## Search, filters, and the archive

Add search when a person with the question can name a word you also use. Search is a failure if your guides say "onboarding" and your readers say "getting started." Pick the reader's word in titles and groups, then let search match it.

Filters help when you have two real dimensions. Job, and then format or product line. A filter for every tag you have ever used is a second junk drawer. If a filter has one item, it is not a filter. Remove it.

Keep an archive for everything else, in chronological order, with a clear name. "All writing" is an honest title. Put it in the footer of the resources section, not in the hero. Regular readers and your future self can use it. A buyer in a hurry should not have to scroll through it to find setup.

Paginate the archive. Do not paginate the job groups if you can avoid it. A group should fit the best answers on one view. If it does not, you have too many pieces, or the group is too wide.

Handle the empty state. A new group with one guide should say so, and show that guide. A search with no results should offer the nearest group, not a blank page and a joke. Empty states are part of the information architecture. They are not a polish pass.

## Writing the cards so the groups stay true

A card is a title, a line, and a group. Resist the thumbnail that could sit on any article. If you use an image, it should mark the job or the specific guide. Hanabi's approach on marketing pages is the same standard: a photograph with a subject, not a keyword collage.

Write titles that say the outcome. "What to hand a new warehouse on day one" beats "Our thoughts on operations." You can still sound like yourselves. Specific and human can live in the same line.

Keep the voice consistent with the rest of the site. A homepage that is calm and a resources section that shouts are two brands. The campaign page can be louder for a month. The library should sound like the company the reader will meet in the product or the shop.

Review cards when you add the tenth piece in a group. Read the lines in a column, without opening the articles. If two lines promise the same outcome, merge the pieces or retitle them until a reader can tell them apart. Duplicates are how a good group turns back into a dump.

Set a owner. Someone decides which group a new piece joins, and whether an old piece still belongs. Without an owner, every new post lands on the resources front because that is the default in the CMS. Change the default.

## How this connects to the rest of the site

The homepage should point at one or two groups, not at the word Resources in the abstract. "Start here if you are choosing a plan" is a link. A footer list can carry the rest.

Sales and support should use the same groups. If a salesperson sends a link, it should be a piece that lives on the shelf the buyer can also find. A private PDF and a public guide that disagree will be the thing the buyer remembers.

The stack can stay quiet. What matters is that a non-developer can add a guide to a group without inventing a new layout. On a Hanabi build, that is a content model with a required group, a required summary line, and a preview. The client portal holds the docs and updates after delivery, including the map of groups, so the next writer does not reconstruct it from the live site.

Local shops have a sharper version of the same problem. A visit and a shipment are different jobs, and the site has to give each a path. The piece on [local businesses that also sell online](/blog/local-businesses-that-also-sell-online) is the next read if your resources are really two businesses sharing one homepage.

If the library is still a feed because the groups were never chosen, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful part is a set of offers with boundaries. A resources section deserves the same kindness: a job, a limit, and a next step.
